actions.fyi: The reset is done. Your board now holds 24 things the checks called broken this morning and 2 jobs, against 59 cards written from stale notes yesterday. Nothing needs deciding — but the top of the list is worth a look, because it is now an ordered claim about what is actually wrong with the game.

status.now: The board was emptied and refilled from a single full run of the checks: 41 of 2222 came back red, and every one of them is on the board with the number it failed on. Cards can no longer be written by hand — a job is poured whole, goal and steps together, and the board refuses one that cannot say what makes it real today or how a machine will tell it is finished.
status.next_up: Retire the twelve handover notes into the documents that own their facts — poured, proven, and next on the list.

blocks.label: One thing you should know
blocks.text: Switching the board on made a single entry in the project history, and it swept up edits another session had in flight in two settings files. Nothing was lost and nothing was overwritten — the work is intact and simply recorded earlier than its author intended. It was a one-off at setup and cannot repeat.

content.label: Why the first 59 cards were binned
content.lead: You are right, and the cause is worth naming: I filled the board from the handover notes instead of from the work.

items: The notes are months of running commentary. A line written in July saying something is broken is evidence about July, not about today — and I carried those lines across as if they were current.

One card describes the black strip at the top of diagnostic pictures as a defect. It is deliberate, it was already diagnosed, and it is sitting on another of your pages as a question waiting for your answer. That card should never have existed.
No card says how we would know it is finished, so nothing on the board can ever be closed with confidence.
The notes' own language came with them, which is why they read as confusing rather than as jobs.

blocks.text: The fix is not to edit 59 cards. It is to bin them, fix the shape a card must have, and let only confirmed work back on.

content.label: What a job looks like from now on
content.lead: Two kinds of card, and only two. A find is one line and takes seconds. A job has a fixed spine, and the board itself pours it — nobody assembles one by hand.

a card nobody can picture is a card nobody picks up

blocks.text: A small job — a stale line of text, a rename — pours a five-step spine: prove, build, verify, record. Grounding, design and review appear only where the work touches how the game looks or behaves. Nothing else may be dropped.

items: A find stays one command with no spine, because friction there is exactly what would kill your first rule. It records which job found it, so you can see what work breeds work.
A find cannot be worked until it is turned into a job, which pours the spine.

blocks.text: The spine is the shape, not the work. What the design step actually decides to build hangs underneath the step it belongs to, added while that step is being worked — nobody can know those items up front. A card with work broken out under it stops being claimable and finishes when its children do, which is the same rule that stops a goal being closed over unfinished parts.

content.label: What each state means, and what moves a card into it
content.lead: You asked where each state is enforced. It was not, beyond taking a job; it is now. The rule that makes it possible: every commit names the card it belongs to.

blocks.text: The one exception: a card that was never going to produce code — a question you answered, a find that turned out not to be real — is marked as such and closes on its reason alone. Marking it is a deliberate act that shows on your screen.

blocks.text: Each of these is a single line on the board, not a plan. It becomes a job — with its proof, its definition of done and its steps — at the moment someone picks it up, and not before. That is what keeps the board from filling with confident guesses again.
Anything an agent notices outside the job it is doing becomes a card, there and then. No exceptions.

blocks.label: Why this one is the whole game
blocks.text: A bug seen in passing, a shortcut someone took, a note that lies about the code, a step that got slower — today that either interrupts the job or evaporates. Filed instead, it costs eight seconds and it is still there next week.

blocks.label: Already half built
blocks.text: This project already refuses to end a session whose closing words push work onto a future one. That same gate becomes the filing gate: the words stop being blocked and start demanding a card.

content.label: One board, and your worktree worry is smaller than I said

blocks.text: Every working copy of this project already shares one board — the tool looks up from the working copy and finds the same one.

blocks.label: Why that holds
blocks.text: The work list is not stored as files that ride along with a branch, so branching cannot fork it. My earlier answer sent it to your home folder; that is only needed to share one board between different projects, which we do not want anyway.

blocks.label: The one setting that matters
blocks.text: Out of the box only one agent may write at a time. With a fleet it runs in shared mode instead, where many write at once. Same single board, one flag at setup.

content.label: Your screen
content.lead: You asked which of the two is steadier. Both are free, both built by outsiders, both run here.

rows: 6 months
16 published versions
2 months
none — built from source

blocks.label: Why that way round
blocks.text: Scotty is prettier and is being worked on harder, but ships no ready-made download and carries seven open complaints about the board drawing things wrong. The other publishes versions you can pin and has three faults open, none of them about the board itself.

blocks.label: Cheap to be wrong
blocks.text: The jobs live in the board, not in the screen. Swapping screens later costs an afternoon and loses nothing.

items: You stop asking what is running. The screen answers it: who holds what, how long they have held it, what is blocked and on what.
Half-finished work stops being invisible. A job that stalls comes back to the queue by itself within a day, instead of waiting for someone to trip over it.
What you mention for later stops depending on my memory. It becomes a card the moment you say it, in the same place as everything else.
The record of a piece of work sits on its card, searchable, instead of in chat you cannot search.
One cost, honestly: a small service runs in the background whenever agents work, and a gate that misfires will occasionally block a session until I loosen it.

decisions.title: Recommend the shared board, not the file-based one
decisions.why: a board kept as files inside the project is tied to a branch, so each working copy gets its own and nobody sees the whole picture

decisions.title: Rule out the weeks-old one-download tool
decisions.why: almost nobody uses it yet, and the project plan is not the place to gamble

decisions.title: Rule out running a full service like the mature products
decisions.why: nicest screen of all, but a permanent service to keep alive and agent access added as an afterthought

decisions.title: Leave agent-launching tools out of scope
decisions.why: you asked for sight of the work, not another way to start it

decisions.title: One board at the top of this project, shared by every working copy
decisions.why: the tool already finds the same board from every working copy, so nothing needs to move to your home folder

decisions.title: Trial an outsider-built screen before building our own
decisions.why: five are good enough to judge in an afternoon, and the jobs are safe whichever one we keep

decisions.title: Skip the two Apple-only screens
decisions.why: they will not run on this machine

decisions.title: Do not force the file-based option to sit outside the project
decisions.why: it ignores any location outside the project by design, and even forced there it has no lock and no way for an agent to take a card

decisions.title: Run the steadier screen, not the prettier one
decisions.why: published versions you can pin and three open faults, against none and fifteen

decisions.title: One job per card, and every card says how we will know it is done
decisions.why: a card with no finish test is exactly the card that rots

decisions.title: A big job becomes a goal with small children, never one big card
decisions.why: several agents can only work at once on pieces that do not wait on each other

decisions.title: Anything discovered mid-job becomes a card immediately
decisions.why: the alternative is my memory, which is the thing you are trying to stop relying on

decisions.title: Abandoned work comes back on its own, in about a quarter of an hour
decisions.why: the board already holds a job on a short lease that an agent's own activity renews, so a dead session loses its claim by itself; a daily sweep would have been slower and something else to remember

decisions.title: Merging into the main line goes through a single slot
decisions.why: two agents merging at once is the one collision the board cannot prevent on its own

decisions.title: The board owns work state; every handover note and running order retires once it is on
decisions.why: you called it: one home for what is being worked on, and the written docs keep only durable facts

decisions.title: Notes and comments may name the relevant card and nothing more
decisions.why: a list of pending work written anywhere else is a second board, and it will disagree with the first

decisions.title: Anything an agent finds outside its job becomes a card, always
decisions.why: you called this the most important rule, and it is the one that decides whether the board is real or decorative

decisions.title: A session may not finish with the board out of date
decisions.why: a rule nothing checks is a rule that rots

decisions.title: Reporting of our usage back to the tool's makers is switched off
decisions.why: no reason to send anything off this machine, even command names

decisions.title: Your screen answers only to this machine
decisions.why: it started out answering the whole network, which is not what a personal board should do

decisions.title: The board is copied to your private repository storage
decisions.why: you asked for it, and it means a dead disk no longer takes the work list with it

decisions.title: That copy is made when a session finishes, not continuously
decisions.why: one moment to get right, and it is the same moment the finishing gate already checks

decisions.title: Every session works under its own board name
decisions.why: the board hands out a job to a name, and every session on this machine would otherwise share one; each now gets its own, stamped on automatically, which is what makes two agents grabbing the same job impossible rather than merely unlikely

decisions.title: Changing code with no job held ends the turn in a refusal
decisions.why: this is the rule that keeps the board honest — if it can be skipped, the screen you look at slowly becomes fiction

decisions.title: Reporting a problem without filing a card ends the turn in a refusal
decisions.why: your first rule, enforced on the agent's own words: it may not tell you something is broken and walk away from it

decisions.title: The merge command itself is refused to anyone not holding the slot
decisions.why: asking politely in a rulebook does not serialise anything; the command does

decisions.title: The rules a session is given at startup are ours, not the tool's
decisions.why: the tool ships its own briefing, four times longer and contradicting several of your standing orders; ours is a fifth of the size and says only what this project does

decisions.title: The first 59 cards are binned, not edited
decisions.why: they were copied from the handover notes rather than from the work, so they inherit claims that were true months ago; editing them would keep the worst part, which is that nobody knows which are still real

decisions.title: Every job has one fixed spine, and the board pours it
decisions.why: a shape that depends on the agent's mood is not a shape; pouring it from a template makes the structure automatic instead of remembered

decisions.title: A job must say how we will know it is done, or it is refused
decisions.why: without that line a card can be closed on an opinion, which is how a board quietly stops meaning anything

decisions.title: A find stays one line and one command
decisions.why: your most important rule is the one with the most friction to lose; a find that costs an agent a form is a find that goes unreported

decisions.title: A small job drops grounding, design and review — and nothing else
decisions.why: a fixed eight steps on a one-line fix is ceremony, and ceremony is what makes people route around a system

decisions.title: The handover notes are deleted, including the two in front of live agents
decisions.why: their lasting facts move into the document that owns each subject and their state onto the cards those agents hold, so nothing is lost and there is no second board

decisions.title: A job is done only when its change is on the main line
decisions.why: closing on a feeling is how a board turns into decoration; the machine can see whether the change landed, so it decides

decisions.title: Every commit names the card it belongs to
decisions.why: it costs an agent nothing and it is the single fact that lets the board tell written work from landed work, automatically

decisions.title: A card moves to written by itself when its commit appears
decisions.why: the state you most want to see — done but not yet landed — is exactly the one an agent would forget to set

decisions.title: A card that produces no code closes on its reason, but must be marked
decisions.why: questions and false alarms are real work and must be closable, while an unmarked card closing without a change would reopen the loophole

decisions.title: Only work the machine confirmed today goes on the board
decisions.why: the 59 binned cards were all plausible; what they were missing was anyone checking they were still true

decisions.title: Cards are poured from one template, never written by hand
decisions.why: every field that makes a card usable is one an agent in a hurry will skip, so the only way in is a command that cannot skip them

decisions.title: Something noticed is filed as a find, and cannot be worked until promoted
decisions.why: filing has to cost seconds or agents stop doing it, and promoting is where the proof and the definition of done get demanded

decisions.title: A card with work broken out under it cannot be claimed
decisions.why: it makes a goal finish when its parts do rather than when someone decides, and it is the same rule at every level of the tree

next.if_nothing: The board is on, enforced, and true as of this morning. Left alone it decays slowly: a check that goes green on its own leaves a card behind that still reads as real.
